gradckpt.d:
Gradient checkpointing trades extra computation for lower memory by storing only some intermediate activations during the forward pass and recomputing the rest during the backward pass. Backpropagation normally keeps every layer's activations so it can compute gradients, and for deep networks with long sequences this activation memory often exceeds the memory used by the weights themselves.

With checkpointing, the network is split into segments and only the inputs to each segment are saved. When the backward pass reaches a segment, that segment's forward computation is run again to rebuild its activations, and then gradients flow through it. Checkpointing every transformer block typically costs about one extra forward pass, roughly 20–35% more training time, while cutting activation memory sharply. It is the standard way to fit larger batches or longer contexts on a fixed GPU. A common misconception is that it saves weight or optimizer memory; it only reduces activation memory, so it is usually combined with sharding or mixed precision.
gradckpt.f: Memory ≈ O(√L) activations for L layers with √L checkpoints (vs. O(L))
u: Fine-tuning large LLMs on a single GPU
Training with long sequence lengths
Increasing batch size under fixed memory

They accept the longer wall-clock time because the alternative was renting larger accelerators.

parallelism.d:
Large models are trained across many accelerators by splitting either the data, the individual weight matrices, or the sequence of layers. In data parallelism, every device holds a full model replica, processes a different slice of the batch, and gradients are averaged with an all-reduce before each update. Sharded variants such as ZeRO and FSDP also split optimizer states, gradients and weights so that no device stores a full copy.

Tensor parallelism splits a single matrix multiplication across devices, for example by columns in the first MLP layer and by rows in the second, so each device computes part of every layer; it needs fast interconnect because it communicates inside each layer. Pipeline parallelism assigns consecutive layers to different devices and streams micro-batches through them. Real systems combine all three. A key pitfall of pipeline parallelism is the pipeline bubble: devices sit idle while the pipeline fills and drains, so enough micro-batches are needed to keep utilization high.
parallelism.f: Pipeline bubble fraction ≈ (p − 1) / (m + p − 1), p stages, m micro-batches
u: Pretraining models too large for one GPU
Scaling training throughput across a cluster
Serving huge models across multiple GPUs
parallelism.x: A foundation-model team trains a large LLM on thousands of GPUs, using tensor parallelism within each 8-GPU node, pipeline parallelism across nodes, and data parallelism across replicas. This layout keeps the communication-heavy tensor-parallel traffic on fast intra-node links. They tune the number of micro-batches to keep the pipeline bubble small.

import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.distributed.fsdp import FullyShardedDataParallel as FSDP

# launch: torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 train.py
dist.init_process_group("nccl")
rank = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])
torch.cuda.set_device(rank)

model = torch.nn.Transformer(d_model=1024, nhead=16).cuda()
# FSDP shards params, grads and optimizer states across ranks (data parallel)
model = FSDP(model)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)

src = torch.randn(32, 16, 1024, device="cuda")  # each rank gets its own data shard
tgt = torch.randn(32, 16, 1024, device="cuda")
loss = model(src, tgt).pow(2).mean()
loss.backward()   # gradients are reduce-scattered across ranks
opt.step()
dist.destroy_process_group()

greedy.d:
Greedy decoding generates text by choosing the single most probable next token at every step. The model produces a probability distribution over the vocabulary, the argmax token is appended to the sequence, and the process repeats until an end token or a length limit is reached.

Because it involves no randomness, greedy decoding is deterministic for a fixed model and prompt (up to small numerical differences on GPUs), which makes it useful for evaluation, code completion, extraction tasks and any setting where reproducibility matters. It is also the cheapest decoding strategy. Its main limitation is that locally best choices do not guarantee the most probable full sequence: a slightly less likely token early on can lead to a much better continuation. In open-ended generation, greedy decoding also tends to produce repetitive loops and bland text, which is why sampling methods with temperature, top-k or top-p are usually preferred for creative or conversational output.

Structured extraction into fixed JSON formats
Short code completions in an IDE

import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

name = "gpt2"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name).eval()

ids = tok("The capital of France is", return_tensors="pt").input_ids
with torch.no_grad():
    for _ in range(10):
        logits = model(ids).logits[:, -1, :]          # next-token logits
        next_id = logits.argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)  # pick the most likely token
        ids = torch.cat([ids, next_id], dim=-1)
        if next_id.item() == tok.eos_token_id:

text = tok.decode(ids[0])

# equivalent built-in call
out = model.generate(tok("Hello", return_tensors="pt").input_ids,
                     do_sample=False, max_new_tokens=10)

beam.d:
Beam search is a decoding algorithm that keeps the B most probable partial sequences at each step instead of only the single best one. At every step, each of the B beams is extended with candidate next tokens, all extensions are scored by their cumulative log-probability, and only the top B are kept. When beams finish with an end token, the highest-scoring complete sequence is returned.

Keeping several hypotheses lets the search recover from an early choice that looked good locally but led nowhere, so beam search usually finds sequences with higher total likelihood than greedy decoding. It works well for tasks with one mostly correct answer, such as machine translation, summarization and speech recognition. Raw log-probability favors short outputs, so a length penalty is normally applied. A well-known limitation is that higher likelihood does not mean better text: for open-ended generation, beam search produces generic, repetitive output, and larger beams can even reduce quality.
beam.f: score(y) = Σ_t log p(y_t | y_<t, x) / |y|^α
u: Neural machine translation output decoding

Speech recognition transcript decoding

temperature.d:
Temperature is a scalar that controls how random sampling from a language model is, by dividing the logits before the softmax. A temperature below 1 sharpens the distribution so that likely tokens become even more likely; a temperature above 1 flattens it so that unlikely tokens get more probability mass. As temperature approaches 0, sampling becomes equivalent to greedy decoding, and at exactly 1 the model's original distribution is used.

Practitioners lower the temperature for factual question answering, code and extraction, where consistency matters, and raise it for brainstorming or creative writing, where diversity is useful. Temperature is often combined with top-k or top-p truncation, which removes the long tail of very unlikely tokens that high temperature would otherwise expose. A common misconception is that temperature changes what the model knows or makes it more creative in a deep sense; it only reshapes the existing distribution, and very high values mostly produce incoherent text.
temperature.f: p_i = exp(z_i / T) / Σ_j exp(z_j / T)

Diverse candidates for creative writing tools
Calibrating confidence of classifier probabilities

The same company's customer-support assistant runs at temperature 0.2 to keep answers consistent with policy. Both settings were chosen by comparing human ratings on sampled outputs.

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

logits = torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0, 0.5, -1.0])

def sample_with_temperature(logits, T):
    if T == 0:
        return int(logits.argmax())             # T -> 0 equals greedy
    probs = F.softmax(logits / T, dim=-1)       # divide logits by T
    return int(torch.multinomial(probs, 1))

for T in [0.2, 1.0, 2.0]:
    probs = F.softmax(logits / T, dim=-1)
    # low T: peaked distribution, high T: flatter distribution
    entropy = -(probs * probs.log()).sum()

token = sample_with_temperature(logits, T=0.7)

topk.d:
Top-k sampling restricts each generation step to the k most probable tokens, renormalizes their probabilities, and samples from that reduced set. All other tokens receive zero probability, so the model can never pick a token from the long tail of the vocabulary, where many individually rare but collectively frequent nonsense tokens live.

This simple truncation produces more coherent text than sampling from the full distribution while still allowing variety, which made it popular for early open-ended generation systems. Typical values range from about 20 to 100, often combined with a temperature. The main weakness is that k is fixed regardless of the shape of the distribution. When the model is very confident, for example after "The capital of France is", a large k still admits poor candidates; when many continuations are reasonable, a small k cuts off valid options. Top-p sampling was introduced largely to address this by adapting the candidate set size to the model's confidence.
topk.f: p'(v) = p(v) / Σ_{u∈V_k} p(u) for v ∈ V_k (top-k tokens), else 0

Generating diverse synthetic training data
Limiting tail tokens in chat assistants

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def top_k_sample(logits, k=40, temperature=1.0):
    logits = logits / temperature
    topk_vals, topk_idx = torch.topk(logits, k)       # keep k largest logits
    probs = F.softmax(topk_vals, dim=-1)              # renormalize over the k tokens
    choice = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1)  # sample within the top k
    return topk_idx.gather(-1, choice)

vocab_logits = torch.randn(1, 50_000)
next_token = top_k_sample(vocab_logits, k=40, temperature=0.8)

# Hugging Face equivalent:
# model.generate(ids, do_sample=True, top_k=40, temperature=0.8)

topp.d:
Top-p sampling, also called nucleus sampling, samples the next token from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches a threshold p. Tokens are sorted by probability, added one by one until their total mass is at least p, the rest are discarded, and the kept probabilities are renormalized before sampling.

The key advantage over top-k is adaptivity. When the model is confident, the nucleus may contain only one or two tokens, so output stays precise; when many continuations are plausible, the nucleus grows and allows variety. Values between 0.8 and 0.95 are common, usually together with a temperature, and it is a default in many chat APIs. A frequent misunderstanding is the order of operations: temperature is applied to the logits first, which changes the distribution and therefore the size of the nucleus. Also, p = 1 disables truncation entirely, and very low p behaves almost like greedy decoding.
topp.f: V_p = smallest set with Σ_{v∈V_p} p(v) ≥ p; sample from p restricted to V_p
u: Default sampling for conversational assistants
Creative writing with controlled diversity
Generating paraphrases for data augmentation
topp.x: A writing-assistant product samples suggestions with top-p = 0.9 and temperature 0.7. Because the nucleus shrinks when the model is confident, grammar fixes stay stable while open-ended rewrites still vary. The team logs the average nucleus size to detect prompts where outputs become erratic.
topp.c:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def top_p_sample(logits, p=0.9, temperature=1.0):
    probs = F.softmax(logits / temperature, dim=-1)
    sorted_p, sorted_idx = probs.sort(descending=True)
    cum = sorted_p.cumsum(dim=-1)
    # drop tokens once cumulative mass before them already exceeds p
    remove = (cum - sorted_p) > p
    sorted_p[remove] = 0.0
    sorted_p = sorted_p / sorted_p.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)  # renormalize
    choice = torch.multinomial(sorted_p, 1)
    return sorted_idx.gather(-1, choice)

logits = torch.randn(1, 32_000)
tok_id = top_p_sample(logits, p=0.9, temperature=0.7)
# HF: model.generate(ids, do_sample=True, top_p=0.9, temperature=0.7)

specdec.d:
Speculative decoding speeds up LLM generation by letting a small, fast draft model propose several tokens, which the large target model then verifies in a single forward pass. Autoregressive decoding is usually limited by memory bandwidth rather than compute, so checking k proposed tokens in parallel costs about the same as generating one.

Each drafted token is accepted with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), where p is the target model's probability and q the draft's. At the first rejection, a replacement token is sampled from the normalized residual distribution max(0, p − q), and drafting restarts. This rejection scheme guarantees that the output has exactly the same distribution as sampling from the target model alone, so quality is unchanged. Speedups of 2–3x are common when the draft model agrees often with the target. The benefit shrinks when acceptance rates are low, when batch sizes are large enough that the system becomes compute-bound, or when the draft model's own latency is not small.
specdec.f: accept x̃ with prob. min(1, p(x̃)/q(x̃)); on reject sample from norm(max(0, p − q))
u: Lowering latency of interactive chat responses
Faster code completion with large models
Cheaper serving of large models at low batch
specdec.x: A coding-assistant team pairs a large code model with a small draft model from the same family that shares its tokenizer. Because code is highly predictable, most drafted tokens are accepted and completion latency drops noticeably. They monitor the acceptance rate per language, since it falls for less common languages.

import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("EleutherAI/pythia-1.4b")
target = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("EleutherAI/pythia-1.4b")
draft = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("EleutherAI/pythia-160m")  # same tokenizer

ids = tok("def fibonacci(n):", return_tensors="pt").input_ids
out = target.generate(ids, assistant_model=draft, max_new_tokens=64, do_sample=False)
code = tok.decode(out[0])

# core acceptance rule for one drafted token x
def accept(p_target, q_draft, x):
    ratio = (p_target[x] / q_draft[x]).clamp(max=1.0)
    if torch.rand(()) < ratio:
        return x
    residual = (p_target - q_draft).clamp(min=0)
    return int(torch.multinomial(residual / residual.sum(), 1))

pagedattn.d:
PagedAttention is an attention implementation that stores the key-value cache in fixed-size blocks that do not need to be contiguous in GPU memory, similar to virtual memory pages in an operating system.

Without paging, a server must reserve a contiguous KV-cache region for each request sized for the maximum possible output length, which wastes much of the memory through over-reservation and fragmentation. With PagedAttention, each sequence has a block table mapping logical token positions to physical blocks, and new blocks are allocated only as tokens are generated. The attention kernel reads keys and values through this table. Near-zero waste means more requests fit in memory at once, which raises throughput substantially. Blocks can also be shared between sequences, such as a common system prompt, with copy-on-write when they diverge. PagedAttention does not reduce the size of the KV cache per token; it only removes wasted space, so long contexts still consume a lot of memory.
pagedattn.f: physical_block = block_table[seq][⌊pos / B⌋], offset = pos mod B

Sharing system prompts across concurrent requests
Parallel sampling and beam search memory sharing

The team tunes the GPU memory fraction reserved for the cache and monitors preemptions when memory runs out.

    model="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct",
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.90,   # share of GPU memory for weights + KV blocks
    block_size=16,
    enable_prefix_caching=True,    # reuse KV blocks of shared prompt prefixes
)

contbatch.d:
Continuous batching, also called in-flight or iteration-level batching, schedules LLM inference one decoding step at a time, so new requests can join the running batch and finished requests can leave it at every step. Static batching, in contrast, waits until every sequence in a batch has finished before starting the next batch.

Because output lengths vary widely, static batching leaves GPU slots idle while short requests wait for the longest one to finish, and new requests queue in the meantime. With continuous batching, the scheduler checks after each forward pass which sequences emitted an end token, removes them, and inserts waiting requests. This keeps the GPU busy and greatly increases throughput while also lowering average queueing delay. It needs careful KV-cache memory management, which is why it is usually paired with PagedAttention. A limitation is that mixing long prefills with decodes can cause latency spikes for running requests, which chunked prefill is designed to reduce.
u: Serving chat APIs with variable-length outputs
Maximizing GPU throughput for batch inference
Reducing queueing delay under bursty traffic

Short answers no longer wait for long essays in the same batch, so time-to-first-token improves under load. The team caps the maximum number of concurrent sequences to protect per-token latency.

longctx.d:
Long context extension refers to techniques that let a pretrained LLM handle sequences much longer than its original training length. Models with rotary position embeddings (RoPE) fail beyond their trained length mainly because they encounter rotation angles they never saw, so most methods rescale positions or frequencies into a familiar range.

Position Interpolation linearly compresses positions by the extension factor. NTK-aware scaling instead increases the RoPE base so that high-frequency dimensions, which encode local order, are barely changed while low-frequency dimensions are stretched. YaRN combines a per-frequency interpolation schedule with an attention temperature adjustment. These methods work best with a short fine-tuning phase on long documents. A key limitation is that a model accepting 128K tokens does not necessarily use them well: retrieval accuracy often drops for information placed in the middle of the context, so long-context ability should be measured with realistic tasks, not only perplexity.
longctx.f: θ_i' = (b·s^{d/(d−2)})^{−2i/d} (NTK-aware RoPE, scale s, base b)

Repository-level code understanding and editing
Summarizing long meeting transcripts and books

prompting.d:
Prompt engineering is the practice of designing the input text given to a language model so that it reliably produces the desired output without changing its weights. A prompt typically combines an instruction, relevant context, constraints on format, and sometimes a few worked examples (few-shot prompting).

Effective prompts state the task explicitly, define the audience and output format, separate instructions from data with clear delimiters, and give examples that cover edge cases. Asking for structured output such as JSON makes downstream parsing robust. Prompt engineering is the fastest and cheapest way to adapt a model, so it is usually tried before retrieval or fine-tuning. The main pitfall is treating prompts as finished after a few manual tests. Small wording changes can shift behavior, and prompts tuned for one model often transfer poorly to another, so prompts should be versioned and evaluated against a fixed test set like any other code.

cot.d:
Chain-of-thought prompting asks a language model to write out intermediate reasoning steps before giving a final answer. It can be triggered with few-shot examples that include worked solutions or simply by an instruction such as "think step by step".

Because a transformer spends a fixed amount of computation per generated token, writing intermediate steps gives the model more computation and lets later tokens condition on earlier partial results, such as a computed subtotal. This substantially improves accuracy on multi-step arithmetic, logic and planning problems, especially for larger models; for small models the gains are much weaker. Two limitations matter in practice. Longer outputs increase latency and cost. More importantly, the written reasoning is not guaranteed to be a faithful account of how the model reached its answer: models can produce plausible steps that do not actually determine the result, so a chain of thought should not be treated as a reliable explanation.
cot.f: p(y | x) = Σ_r p(r | x)·p(y | x, r), r = reasoning chain

Complex reasoning over business rules
Debugging and planning code changes

Only the final field is shown to users, while the reasoning is logged for reviewers. Accuracy on their internal test cases improved compared with direct answers, at the cost of longer responses.

selfcons.d:
Self-consistency improves chain-of-thought reasoning by sampling several independent reasoning paths for the same question and choosing the final answer that appears most often. Instead of trusting one greedy chain, the model is run with a nonzero temperature N times, each final answer is extracted, and a majority vote decides.

The intuition is that a hard problem may have many valid reasoning routes that converge on the same correct answer, while errors tend to scatter across different wrong answers. Marginalizing over reasoning paths therefore gives a more reliable estimate than any single path. It brings large gains on arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks. The obvious cost is N times more inference. It also requires answers that can be compared exactly, such as numbers or multiple-choice labels; for free-form text, voting needs a similarity measure or an LLM judge, and if the model is systematically wrong, more samples only reinforce the same mistake.
u: Boosting accuracy on math reasoning tasks
Confidence estimation from answer agreement
Robust multiple-choice question answering
selfcons.x: An education platform grades generated math solutions by sampling ten reasoning paths and voting on the final number. When agreement falls below a threshold, the problem is routed to a human tutor instead of being auto-answered. The extra inference cost is limited because only flagged problems use the full ten samples.

from collections import Counter
import re
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()
q = "If 4 workers build a wall in 6 days, how many days do 3 workers need?"
prompt = f"{q}\nThink step by step. End with 'Answer: <number>'."

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    temperature=0.8,     # diversity between reasoning paths
    n=10,                # sample 10 independent chains
)
answers = []
for choice in resp.choices:
    m = re.search(r"Answer:\s*([-\d.]+)", choice.message.content)
    if m:
        answers.append(m.group(1))
best, votes = Counter(answers).most_common(1)[0]
confidence = votes / len(answers)    # agreement rate as a confidence score

tot.d:
Tree of Thoughts is a prompting framework in which a language model explores many partial reasoning steps as a search tree instead of following a single linear chain. Each node is a "thought", a coherent intermediate step such as a candidate equation or a plan fragment.

At each node, the model proposes several next thoughts, then evaluates them by scoring or voting. A search algorithm such as breadth-first search with a fixed beam width, or depth-first search with backtracking, expands the most promising states and prunes the rest. This allows lookahead and backtracking, which plain chain-of-thought cannot do, and it gives large improvements on puzzles with clear intermediate checks, such as the Game of 24 or crosswords. The cost is many more model calls per problem, and the approach depends on the model being able to judge partial progress reliably. For most everyday tasks, simpler sampling with self-consistency is cheaper and good enough.
tot.f: S_{t+1} = top_b { s' ∈ propose(s), s ∈ S_t } ranked by V(s')
u: Solving combinatorial puzzles like Game of 24
Multi-step planning with backtracking
Exploring alternative designs before committing
tot.x: A logistics research team uses a tree-of-thoughts loop to draft delivery schedules, where the model proposes partial assignments and a rule-based checker scores constraint violations. Combining the model's proposals with a deterministic evaluator made pruning far more reliable than self-evaluation alone. The approach is used offline because each plan needs many model calls.
tot.c:
def tree_of_thoughts(problem, llm, steps=3, k=5, beam=3):
    frontier = [""]                                  # partial solutions
    for _ in range(steps):
        candidates = []
        for state in frontier:
            # propose k possible next thoughts from this state
            prompt = f"Problem: {problem}\nSteps so far:\n{state}\nPropose next step:"
            for thought in llm.sample(prompt, n=k, temperature=0.7):
                candidates.append(state + thought + "\n")
        # evaluate each candidate state with the model as a judge
        scored = []
        for cand in candidates:
            verdict = llm.complete(
                f"Problem: {problem}\nPartial solution:\n{cand}\n"
                "Can this still reach a correct answer? Reply with a score 1-10:")
            scored.append((float(verdict.strip() or 0), cand))
        scored.sort(key=lambda t: t[0], reverse=True)
        frontier = [c for _, c in scored[:beam]]     # keep the best b states
    return frontier[0]

rag.d:
Retrieval-augmented generation answers a query by first retrieving relevant documents from an external knowledge source and then giving them to a language model as context for generating the answer. It lets a model use private or up-to-date information that was not in its training data, without retraining.

A typical pipeline splits documents into chunks, embeds each chunk, and stores the vectors in an index. At query time, the question is embedded, the nearest chunks are retrieved (often combined with keyword search such as BM25), optionally reranked with a cross-encoder, and inserted into the prompt with an instruction to answer only from the provided sources and cite them. RAG reduces hallucination on knowledge-heavy tasks and makes answers traceable. Its quality is limited by retrieval: if the right chunk is not retrieved, the model cannot use it, and poorly chosen chunk sizes or missing metadata cause many failures. Retrieval recall and answer faithfulness should therefore be evaluated separately.
rag.f: p(y | q) ≈ LLM(y | q, top_k_{d∈D} sim(E(q), E(d)))

from openai import OpenAI

        "VPN access requires a hardware token.",
        "Expense reports are due within 30 days."]

          f"Sources:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}")

vectordb.d:
Vector search finds the stored vectors most similar to a query vector, and approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms make this fast at large scale by giving up exactness. Exact search compares the query with every vector, which is too slow for millions or billions of embeddings at low latency.

The main ANN families are graph-based, partition-based and compression-based. HNSW builds a layered proximity graph and greedily walks it from coarse to fine layers. IVF clusters vectors with k-means and searches only the few clusters nearest to the query. Product quantization compresses each vector into short codes so that distances can be estimated cheaply and indexes fit in memory. Each index exposes a parameter, such as efSearch or nprobe, that trades recall for speed. A frequent mistake is assuming ANN results are exact: recall@k should be measured against brute-force search, and metadata filters applied after the ANN step can silently return too few results.
u: Semantic search over document embeddings
Product and content recommendation retrieval
Deduplication of near-identical images or text

The team tuned efSearch so recall against exact search stays high while latency remains within the page-load budget. import numpy as np
import faiss

d = 384
xb = np.random.rand(100_000, d).astype("float32")   # database vectors
xq = np.random.rand(5, d).astype("float32")         # query vectors
faiss.normalize_L2(xb); faiss.normalize_L2(xq)      # cosine via inner product

# IVF index: k-means into 1024 cells, search only nprobe of them
quantizer = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d)
index = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(quantizer, d, 1024, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)
index.train(xb)
index.add(xb)
index.nprobe = 16                                   # recall/speed trade-off
D, I = index.search(xq, 10)

# measure recall against exact search
exact = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d); exact.add(xb)
_, I_exact = exact.search(xq, 10)
recall = np.mean([len(set(a) & set(b)) / 10 for a, b in zip(I, I_exact)])

embedmodel.d:
A text embedding model maps a piece of text to a fixed-length vector so that texts with similar meaning lie close together, usually measured by cosine similarity. Modern embedding models are transformer encoders whose token outputs are pooled, for example by averaging or by taking a special token, into one vector.

They are trained with contrastive learning: pairs of related texts, such as a question and its answer, are pulled together while other texts in the batch act as negatives and are pushed apart. Embeddings power semantic search, retrieval for RAG, clustering, deduplication and as features for lightweight classifiers. Important practical details are that query and document embeddings must come from the same model, some models require task prefixes such as "query:" and "passage:", and inputs longer than the model's maximum length are truncated. Similarity scores are only meaningful relative to each other within one model, not as absolute probabilities.

rerank.d:
Reranking is a second retrieval stage that re-scores a small set of candidate documents with a more accurate but more expensive model. A fast first stage, such as BM25 or vector search, returns perhaps 50–200 candidates, and the reranker reorders them so that the best few are passed to the user or to an LLM.

The most common reranker is a cross-encoder, a transformer that reads the query and one document together and outputs a relevance score. Because attention operates across both texts jointly, it captures fine-grained interactions such as negation or exact entity matches that independent bi-encoder embeddings miss. Reranking usually brings a large precision gain in RAG and search pipelines for modest extra latency. Its limitation is that it can only reorder what the first stage retrieved: it cannot recover a relevant document that was never in the candidate set, and its cost grows linearly with the number of candidates.

agent.d:
An LLM agent is a system in which a language model repeatedly decides what action to take next, executes it through tools, observes the result, and continues until a goal is reached. Instead of producing one answer, the model runs in a loop with memory of previous steps and access to functions such as search, code execution, databases or APIs.

Typical components are a system prompt describing the goal and available tools, a loop that feeds tool results back into the context, a stopping condition. Agents suit open-ended tasks whose steps cannot be fixed in advance, such as debugging code or multi-source research. The main limitation is reliability: errors compound over many steps, so a small per-step failure rate becomes a large task failure rate. Production agents therefore need step limits, cost budgets, sandboxed tools, human approval for risky actions, and logging of complete trajectories for evaluation, since prompt injection through tool outputs is a real security risk.
agent.f: a_t ~ π_LLM(a | goal, o_1, a_1, …, o_{t−1}); o_t = env(a_t)

Multi-source research and report writing

                   "required": ["city"]}}}]

tooluse.d:
Function calling lets a language model request the execution of external functions by emitting a structured call, usually JSON with a function name and arguments, instead of plain text. The application declares available tools with names, descriptions and JSON Schema parameters; the model decides whether to call one, the application runs it, and the result is returned to the model as a new message.

Models are fine-tuned to produce well-formed calls and to choose tools based on their descriptions, so clear tool names, precise descriptions and tight schemas strongly affect accuracy. Function calling connects LLMs to databases, calculators, search engines and business APIs, and it is the basic building block of agents. A key misconception is that the model executes the function itself; it only proposes the call, and the application is responsible for validating arguments, enforcing permissions and handling errors, because models can produce wrong or hallucinated arguments.

Booking and order actions in assistants

react.d:
ReAct is a prompting pattern in which a language model interleaves reasoning traces with actions, alternating between "Thought", "Action" and "Observation" steps. The model first writes a thought about what it needs, then issues an action such as a search query or a tool call, receives an observation from the environment, and uses it in the next thought.

Combining the two addresses weaknesses of each alone. Pure chain-of-thought reasoning can hallucinate facts because it never checks the outside world, while pure action sequences lack a plan and struggle to recover from unexpected results. With ReAct, the reasoning steers which actions to take, and the observations ground the reasoning in retrieved facts. It was shown to improve multi-hop question answering and interactive tasks, and its loop structure underlies most modern agent frameworks. Limitations include long contexts as trajectories grow, loops where the model repeats the same action, and sensitivity to noisy observations, so step limits and output parsing safeguards are needed.
u: Multi-hop question answering with web search
Interactive troubleshooting with diagnostic tools
Grounded fact-checking of generated claims
react.x: An IT operations team uses a ReAct-style assistant that reasons about an alert, queries logs and metrics through tools, and summarizes the likely root cause. Observations from real systems keep the reasoning grounded, and every action is read-only. Engineers see the full thought-action trace, which makes it easier to judge whether to trust the conclusion.
react.c:
import re

PROMPT = '''Answer the question using these actions:
Search[query] -> returns a text snippet
Finish[answer] -> returns the final answer
Use the format: Thought: ... Action: ...
Question: {q}
'''

def react(question, llm, search, max_steps=6):
    trace = PROMPT.format(q=question)
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        step = llm(trace, stop=["Observation:"])     # model writes Thought + Action
        trace += step
        m = re.search(r"Action:\s*(\w+)\[(.*)\]", step)
        if not m:
            break
        action, arg = m.groups()
        if action == "Finish":
            return arg
        observation = search(arg)                     # act in the environment
        trace += f"\nObservation: {observation}\n"
    return None

ttc.d:
Reasoning models are language models trained to spend extra computation at inference time, usually by generating a long internal chain of thought before answering, and test-time compute refers to scaling that inference effort to improve accuracy. Instead of only making models bigger, quality is raised by letting them think longer on harder problems.

These models are typically trained with reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable rewards, such as math problems with known answers or code with unit tests. Through this training, behaviors like decomposing problems, checking intermediate results and backtracking emerge in the reasoning trace. Test-time compute can also be scaled externally with parallel sampling and majority voting, best-of-N selection with a verifier. Accuracy on math and coding often rises steadily with more reasoning tokens. The trade-offs are higher latency and cost per query, and overthinking: for simple questions, long reasoning adds expense without benefit and can even introduce errors, so many systems let users set a reasoning-effort budget.
ttc.f: Accuracy ≈ a + b·log(test-time compute) (empirical trend, within a range)

llmeval.d:
LLM evaluation measures how well a language model performs on tasks of interest, using standardized benchmarks, task-specific test sets, human judgments and model-based judges. Public benchmarks cover knowledge (MMLU), math (GSM8K, MATH), code (HumanEval, SWE-bench) and preference-based ranking (Chatbot Arena), giving common reference points for comparing models.

Evaluation methods differ by task type. Multiple-choice benchmarks compare log-probabilities or extracted letters; code is checked by running unit tests, reported as pass@k; open-ended answers are scored by humans or by an LLM-as-a-judge with a rubric, often through pairwise comparison. For production systems, the most valuable evaluation is a custom test set built from real user queries with clear pass criteria, run automatically on every model or prompt change. Key pitfalls are data contamination, where benchmark items appeared in training data and inflate scores, sensitivity to prompt format, and judge biases toward longer answers or a fixed position, which must be controlled by swapping order and calibrating against human labels.

import numpy as np
from math import comb

def pass_at_k(n, c, k):
    """Unbiased pass@k: n samples generated, c passed the tests."""
    if n - c < k:
        return 1.0
    return 1.0 - comb(n - c, k) / comb(n, k)

# results per problem: (samples generated, samples passing unit tests)
results = [(20, 3), (20, 0), (20, 12), (20, 20)]
p1 = np.mean([pass_at_k(n, c, 1) for n, c in results])
p10 = np.mean([pass_at_k(n, c, 10) for n, c in results])

# pairwise LLM-as-judge with position swap to reduce order bias
def judge_pair(judge, q, a, b):
    v1 = judge(q, first=a, second=b)    # returns "first" or "second"
    v2 = judge(q, first=b, second=a)
    if v1 == "first" and v2 == "second": return "A"
    if v1 == "second" and v2 == "first": return "B"
    return "tie"

moe.d:
A Mixture of Experts layer replaces one large feed-forward network with many smaller expert networks and a router that sends each token to only a few of them. Total parameter count grows with the number of experts, but compute per token stays close to that of a much smaller dense model, because only the selected experts run.

In transformer LLMs, the MoE layer usually replaces the MLP in some or all blocks. For each token, a learned router scores all experts, the top-k (often 1, 2 or 8 of many) are activated, and their outputs are combined with the router weights. Mixtral and DeepSeek-V3 use this design to gain quality at equal FLOPs. The main costs are memory and communication: all experts must be stored, even if few are used per token, and expert parallelism requires all-to-all traffic between devices. Training also needs load-balancing mechanisms, otherwise the router collapses onto a few experts.
moe.f: y = Σ_{i∈TopK(g(x))} g_i(x)·E_i(x), g(x) = softmax(W_r x)

moe.c:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class MoE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=512, n_experts=8, k=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.k = k
        self.router = nn.Linear(d, n_experts, bias=False)
        self.experts = nn.ModuleList(
            nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(4 * d, d))
            for _ in range(n_experts))

    def forward(self, x):                        # x: (tokens, d)
        logits = self.router(x)
        weights, idx = logits.topk(self.k, dim=-1)  # choose k experts per token
        weights = F.softmax(weights, dim=-1)
        out = torch.zeros_like(x)
        for e, expert in enumerate(self.experts):
            tok, slot = (idx == e).nonzero(as_tuple=True)
            if tok.numel():                      # run expert only on its tokens
                out[tok] += weights[tok, slot, None] * expert(x[tok])
        return out

y = MoE()(torch.randn(16, 512))

router.d:
The router, or gating network, is the small learned component in a Mixture of Experts layer that decides which experts process each token. It is usually a single linear layer that produces one score per expert; the k highest-scoring experts are selected and their outputs are weighted by normalized router scores.

Top-k gating makes computation sparse, since only k experts run per token. Variants differ in when they normalize: some apply softmax over all experts and keep the top-k probabilities, others apply softmax only over the selected k. Noisy top-k gating adds noise during training to encourage exploration, and expert-choice routing reverses the direction so that each expert picks its top tokens. Each expert has a capacity limit per batch; tokens beyond it may be dropped and pass through only the residual connection. A key subtlety is that the top-k selection itself is not differentiable, so experts receive gradient only through the gate weights of tokens they actually processed.
router.f: g(x) = softmax(TopK(W_r x, k)), TopK sets non-top-k entries to −∞

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def top_k_gating(x, W_r, k=2, capacity_factor=1.25, train=True):
    logits = x @ W_r                                  # (tokens, n_experts)
    if train:
        logits = logits + torch.randn_like(logits) * 1e-2   # optional noise
    top_vals, top_idx = logits.topk(k, dim=-1)
    gates = F.softmax(top_vals, dim=-1)               # normalize over chosen k
    n_tokens, n_experts = logits.shape
    capacity = int(capacity_factor * n_tokens * k / n_experts)
    # tokens assigned beyond an expert's capacity are dropped
    load = torch.bincount(top_idx.flatten(), minlength=n_experts)
    overflow = (load - capacity).clamp(min=0)
    return top_idx, gates, overflow

x = torch.randn(64, 256)
W_r = torch.randn(256, 8) * 0.02
idx, gates, overflow = top_k_gating(x, W_r)

loadbal.d:
A load-balancing loss is an auxiliary training objective in Mixture of Experts models that encourages the router to spread tokens evenly across experts. Without it, routing tends to collapse: a few experts get most tokens early in training, become better, and therefore attract even more tokens, while the others stay undertrained.

The common Switch Transformer form multiplies, for each expert, the fraction of tokens actually dispatched to it by the average router probability assigned to it, sums over experts, and scales by the number of experts. The dispatch fraction is not differentiable, but the probability term is, so gradients push probability away from overloaded experts. The loss reaches its minimum of 1 under perfectly uniform routing and is added with a small coefficient, often around 0.01. The main trade-off is that a strong balancing term forces uniform usage and can hurt quality, which motivated auxiliary-loss-free approaches such as DeepSeek-V3's per-expert bias adjustment that only affects selection.
loadbal.f: L_bal = α · N · Σ_{i=1}^{N} f_i · P_i

Improving hardware utilization across expert devices
Reducing dropped tokens under capacity limits
loadbal.x: During pretraining of an MoE model, an engineering team monitors per-expert token fractions alongside the balancing loss. When imbalance appears in deeper layers, they compare raising the loss coefficient with a bias-based balancing scheme, checking validation perplexity to ensure balance is not bought with quality.
loadbal.c:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def load_balancing_loss(router_logits, top_idx, n_experts, alpha=0.01):
    # router_logits: (tokens, n_experts); top_idx: (tokens, k)
    probs = F.softmax(router_logits, dim=-1)
    # f_i: fraction of token assignments dispatched to expert i (no gradient)
    one_hot = F.one_hot(top_idx, n_experts).float().sum(dim=1)
    f = one_hot.mean(dim=0) / top_idx.shape[1]
    # P_i: mean router probability for expert i (differentiable)
    P = probs.mean(dim=0)
    return alpha * n_experts * torch.sum(f * P)

def router_z_loss(router_logits, beta=1e-3):
    # penalize large logits for numerical stability
    return beta * torch.logsumexp(router_logits, dim=-1).pow(2).mean()

logits = torch.randn(128, 8, requires_grad=True)
top_idx = logits.topk(2, dim=-1).indices
aux = load_balancing_loss(logits, top_idx, 8) + router_z_loss(logits)
aux.backward()

finegrained.d:
Fine-grained and shared experts are two refinements of Mixture of Experts design, popularized by DeepSeekMoE, that improve how specialized experts become. Fine-grained segmentation splits each standard expert into several smaller ones and activates proportionally more of them, keeping compute per token the same while greatly increasing the number of possible expert combinations.

Shared experts are a few experts that process every token regardless of routing. They capture common knowledge, such as basic syntax, that every token needs, so routed experts do not each have to learn it redundantly and can specialize more sharply. In DeepSeek-V3, for example, each MoE layer has one shared expert and 256 small routed experts, of which 8 are selected per token. The trade-offs are engineering ones: many tiny experts mean small matrix multiplications that use GPUs less efficiently, more routing overhead and more all-to-all communication, so efficient grouped-GEMM kernels and careful expert placement become important.
finegrained.f: h = x + Σ_{i=1}^{N_s} FFN_i^s(x) + Σ_{j∈TopK} g_j(x)·FFN_j^r(x)

Increasing expert specialization at fixed compute
Reducing redundant knowledge across experts

Teams adopting this design for their own MoE pretraining rely on grouped matrix-multiplication kernels to keep GPUs efficient with small experts. They also limit how many devices each token's experts can span to control communication cost.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

ffn = lambda d, h: nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, h), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(h, d))

class SharedFineMoE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=512, n_shared=1, n_routed=32, k=4, h=256):
        super().__init__()
        self.k = k
        self.shared = nn.ModuleList(ffn(d, h) for _ in range(n_shared))   # always on
        self.routed = nn.ModuleList(ffn(d, h) for _ in range(n_routed))   # small experts
        self.router = nn.Linear(d, n_routed, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):                         # x: (tokens, d)
        out = sum(e(x) for e in self.shared)
        scores = torch.sigmoid(self.router(x))
        w, idx = scores.topk(self.k, dim=-1)
        for e, expert in enumerate(self.routed):
            tok, slot = (idx == e).nonzero(as_tuple=True)
            if tok.numel():
                out[tok] += w[tok, slot, None] * expert(x[tok])
        return x + out

y = SharedFineMoE()(torch.randn(32, 512))

ssm.d:
A state space model processes a sequence by maintaining a hidden state that evolves through a linear recurrence, and S4 (Structured State Space for Sequences) made this approach practical for deep learning on very long sequences. The model is defined by continuous-time matrices A, B, C that are discretized with a step size Δ, giving h_t = Ā h_{t−1} + B̄ x_t and y_t = C h_t.

Because the system is linear and time-invariant, the same computation can be done in two ways: as a recurrence, for fast inference, or as a long convolution over the whole sequence, computed efficiently with FFTs for parallel training. S4 initializes A with the HiPPO matrix so the state stores a compressed input history. It excelled on long-range benchmarks. Its key limitation is that parameters do not depend on the input, so the model cannot selectively ignore or focus on tokens, which hurts performance on language; Mamba was designed to fix this.
ssm.f: h_t = Ā h_{t−1} + B̄ x_t, y_t = C h_t, Ā = exp(ΔA)

Raw audio and speech waveform modeling
Long-range sequence classification tasks

Its convolutional training mode handles sequences of tens of thousands of steps that would be too expensive for full attention. For streaming use, the same model runs in recurrent mode with constant memory per sample.

import torch

def ssm_scan(x, A, B, C, delta):
    """Discretized linear SSM run as a recurrence (diagonal A)."""
    A_bar = torch.exp(delta * A)                 # zero-order hold for A
    B_bar = (A_bar - 1) / A * B                  # ZOH for diagonal A
    h = torch.zeros(A.shape[0])
    ys = []
    for x_t in x:                                # x: (L,) scalar input channel
        h = A_bar * h + B_bar * x_t              # state update
        ys.append((C * h).sum())                 # readout
    return torch.stack(ys)

N, L = 16, 200

B, C = torch.ones(N), torch.randn(N)

# equivalent convolution kernel K_k = C · A_bar^k · B_bar (time-invariant)
A_bar = torch.exp(0.05 * A); B_bar = (A_bar - 1) / A * B
K = torch.stack([(C * A_bar**k * B_bar).sum() for k in range(L)])

mamba.d:
Mamba is a sequence model built on a selective state space model, in which the SSM parameters B, C and the step size Δ are computed from the current input rather than being fixed. This input dependence lets the model decide, token by token, what to write into its state and what to forget.

Selectivity breaks the time-invariance that allowed earlier SSMs such as S4 to be trained as a global convolution. Mamba instead uses a hardware-aware parallel scan that keeps the expanded state in fast on-chip memory, giving training time linear in sequence length. At inference, it runs as a recurrence with a fixed-size state, so memory does not grow with context length and per-token generation cost is constant. Its main limitation is that a fixed-size state cannot store arbitrary amounts of exact information, so tasks that require copying or recalling specific details from far back in the context remain harder than with attention.
mamba.f: h_t = exp(Δ_t A) h_{t−1} + Δ_t B_t x_t, y_t = C_t h_t, (B_t, C_t, Δ_t) = f(x_t)

Fast constant-memory autoregressive generation
Genomics and long DNA sequence modeling

The constant-size recurrent state also keeps inference memory flat. They still evaluate recall-heavy tasks separately, since those are a known weakness of pure SSMs.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class SelectiveSSM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=64, n=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.A_log = nn.Parameter(torch.log(torch.arange(1, n + 1).float()).repeat(d, 1))
        self.to_B, self.to_C = nn.Linear(d, n), nn.Linear(d, n)
        self.to_delta = nn.Linear(d, d)

    def forward(self, x):                      # x: (L, d)
        A = -torch.exp(self.A_log)             # (d, n), negative for stability
        B, C = self.to_B(x), self.to_C(x)      # input-dependent (L, n)
        delta = F.softplus(self.to_delta(x))   # input-dependent step (L, d)
        h = torch.zeros_like(A)
        ys = []
        for t in range(x.shape[0]):            # sequential scan (reference version)
            dA = torch.exp(delta[t, :, None] * A)
            h = dA * h + delta[t, :, None] * B[t] * x[t, :, None]
            ys.append(h @ C[t])
        return torch.stack(ys)                 # (L, d)

y = SelectiveSSM()(torch.randn(100, 64))

rwkv.d:
RWKV is a neural network architecture that combines transformer-style parallel training with recurrent-network inference, using a linear attention mechanism with learned exponential time decay instead of softmax attention. Its name comes from the four main elements in each block: Receptance, Weight (decay), Key and Value.

In the time-mixing block, each channel keeps a running weighted sum of past values, where older tokens are discounted by a learned per-channel decay, and a receptance gate controls how much of this summary is passed on. Because this sum can be updated incrementally, inference runs as an RNN with a constant-size state per layer, so memory and per-token cost do not grow with context length. During training, the same computation can be parallelized over the sequence. Later versions, such as RWKV-6 and RWKV-7, make the decay data-dependent. As with other recurrent designs, the fixed state limits precise recall of details from far back in long contexts.
rwkv.f: wkv_t = (Σ_{i<t} e^{−(t−1−i)w + k_i} v_i + e^{u + k_t} v_t) / (Σ_{i<t} e^{−(t−1−i)w + k_i} + e^{u + k_t})
u: Efficient LLM inference on edge devices
Long-context generation with constant memory
Multilingual open-source language modeling
rwkv.x: A mobile app team evaluating on-device text generation chooses an RWKV model because its memory use stays constant regardless of conversation length. This avoids the growing KV cache that limits transformers on phones. They accept somewhat weaker performance on tasks that need exact recall of long earlier passages.

import torch

def rwkv_time_mix(k, v, w, u):
    """Recurrent RWKV-4 style WKV for one channel set. k, v: (L, d)."""
    L, d = k.shape
    num = torch.zeros(d); den = torch.zeros(d)   # running weighted sums (state)
    decay = torch.exp(-torch.exp(w))            # per-channel decay in (0, 1)
    out = []
    for t in range(L):
        # current token gets a bonus u; past tokens come from the state
        cur = torch.exp(u + k[t])
        out.append((num + cur * v[t]) / (den + cur))
        # update state: decay old contributions, add current token
        num = decay * num + torch.exp(k[t]) * v[t]
        den = decay * den + torch.exp(k[t])
    return torch.stack(out)

L, d = 50, 32
y = rwkv_time_mix(torch.randn(L, d) * 0.1, torch.randn(L, d),
                  w=torch.zeros(d), u=torch.zeros(d))
r = torch.sigmoid(torch.randn(L, d))            # receptance gate
gated = r * y

hybrid.d:
Hybrid architectures interleave attention layers with state space or other recurrent layers in one model, aiming to combine the precise in-context recall of attention with the efficiency of linear-time sequence layers. Jamba, from AI21 Labs, is a well-known example that mixes Mamba layers and transformer attention layers, roughly one attention layer for every seven Mamba layers, and adds Mixture of Experts feed-forward layers.

The intuition is that most layers can process sequence information cheaply with a fixed-size recurrent state, while a few attention layers handle tasks that need exact lookup of earlier tokens, such as copying or retrieval. Because only a small share of layers use attention, the KV cache is several times smaller than in a pure transformer of similar size, which allows very long contexts on limited GPU memory with good throughput. The main challenges are choosing the layer ratio and placement, and the need for specialized kernels and serving support for both layer types.
hybrid.f: KV memory ∝ (n_attn_layers / n_layers) × that of a full transformer

High-throughput serving of long-context models
Combining exact recall with linear-time layers

Compared with a transformer of similar quality, it supports more concurrent long requests. They verify that their serving engine has optimized kernels for the Mamba layers.

mla.d:
Multi-Head Latent Attention is an attention variant introduced in DeepSeek-V2 that greatly reduces KV-cache size by storing a single low-dimensional latent vector per token instead of full keys and values for every head. Keys and values for all heads are reconstructed from this shared latent through learned up-projection matrices.

Each token's hidden state is down-projected to a compressed latent c, which is all that needs to be cached. At inference, the up-projection for keys can be absorbed into the query projection and the one for values into the output projection, so attention can operate directly on the cached latents without materializing full keys and values. Rotary position embeddings do not commute with this absorption, so MLA uses a decoupled design: a small extra key component carries RoPE and is cached separately. MLA reaches a smaller cache than grouped-query attention while matching standard attention quality. The cost is a more complex implementation and extra projection computation.
mla.f: c_t = W_DKV h_t; k_t = W_UK c_t; v_t = W_UV c_t (cache only c_t and k_t^rope)
u: Shrinking KV cache for long-context serving
Higher batch throughput in LLM inference
Efficient attention in large MoE models
mla.x: DeepSeek-V2 and V3 use MLA so that each token's cache entry is a compact latent rather than full per-head keys and values. Serving teams running these models rely on engine support for MLA-specific kernels. The smaller cache lets them hold more concurrent long sequences per GPU.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class MLA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=1024, n_heads=16, d_latent=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.h, self.dh = n_heads, d // n_heads
        self.q_proj = nn.Linear(d, d, bias=False)
        self.kv_down = nn.Linear(d, d_latent, bias=False)  # compress: this is cached
        self.k_up = nn.Linear(d_latent, d, bias=False)     # reconstruct keys
        self.v_up = nn.Linear(d_latent, d, bias=False)     # reconstruct values
        self.out = nn.Linear(d, d, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x, latent_cache=None):           # x: (B, T, d)
        B, T, _ = x.shape; c = self.kv_down(x)        # (B, T, d_latent)
        if latent_cache is not None:
            c = torch.cat([latent_cache, c], dim=1)
        split = lambda t: t.view(B, -1, self.h, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)
        q, k, v = split(self.q_proj(x)), split(self.k_up(c)), split(self.v_up(c))
        o = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=latent_cache is None)
        return self.out(o.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, -1)), c  # return new cache

y, cache = MLA()(torch.randn(2, 10, 1024))  # cache per token: 128 values vs 2 * 1024 for standard multi-head attention

mtp.d:
Multi-token prediction trains a language model to predict several future tokens at each position instead of only the next one. Extra output heads or small extra transformer modules, attached to the shared trunk, predict tokens t+2, t+3 and so on, and their losses are added to the standard next-token loss.

The additional targets give a denser training signal and push the hidden representations to plan further ahead, which has been reported to improve sample efficiency and downstream performance. DeepSeek-V3 uses sequential MTP modules that keep the causal chain by conditioning each extra prediction on the previous depth's representation and the embedding of the next true token. A second benefit appears at inference: the extra heads can act as a built-in draft model for speculative decoding, proposing several tokens that the main head verifies, which speeds up generation. Gains are not universal; small models may see little benefit or even worse results.
mtp.f: L = Σ_t Σ_{k=1}^{K} λ_k · (−log p_k(x_{t+k} | x_{≤t}))
u: Improving sample efficiency in LLM pretraining
Built-in drafts for speculative decoding
Stronger planning signals for code models

At inference, that module can serve as a draft predictor for speculative decoding, and DeepSeek reported a high acceptance rate for the second token. Teams without that serving path simply drop the module after training.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class MTPHeads(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=512, vocab=32000, k=3):
        super().__init__()
        self.k = k
        # one small projection per future offset, sharing the trunk output
        self.heads = nn.ModuleList(nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, d), nn.GELU())
                                   for _ in range(k))
        self.unembed = nn.Linear(d, vocab, bias=False)   # shared output layer

    def loss(self, h, tokens):                # h: (B, T, d) trunk states
        total = 0.0
        for i, head in enumerate(self.heads, start=1):    # predict token t+i
            logits = self.unembed(head(h[:, :-i]))
            target = tokens[:, i:]
            total = total + F.cross_entropy(logits.flatten(0, 1), target.flatten())
        return total / self.k

B, T, d = 2, 64, 512

tokens = torch.randint(0, 32000, (B, T))
MTPHeads(d).loss(h, tokens).backward()

mod.d:
Mixture of Depths is a technique in which each transformer block processes only a selected subset of tokens, while the remaining tokens skip the block through the residual connection. A learned router assigns each token a scalar score, and only the top-k tokens in the sequence pass through the block's attention and MLP.

Because k is fixed in advance, the computation graph has static tensor shapes and a known FLOP budget, which suits accelerators, while the model still learns to spend more compute on harder or more informative tokens. The block output for selected tokens is multiplied by the router score, which keeps the router on the gradient path. The main practical issue is that top-k over the sequence is non-causal, since it depends on future tokens, so autoregressive sampling needs an auxiliary predictor or classifier that decides from the current token alone whether it will be selected.
mod.f: x_i^{l+1} = r_i·f(x̃)_i + x_i if r_i ∈ TopK(r), else x_i

They reach similar validation loss with fewer FLOPs per step. For generation, they train a small causal predictor to approximate the top-k routing decision.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class MoDBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=512, capacity=0.125):
        super().__init__()
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.router = nn.Linear(d, 1)
        self.block = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d, nhead=8, batch_first=True)

    def forward(self, x):                           # x: (B, T, d)
        B, T, d = x.shape
        k = max(1, int(self.capacity * T))
        scores = self.router(x).squeeze(-1)         # (B, T)
        top = scores.topk(k, dim=-1).indices.sort(dim=-1).values  # keep order
        idx = top.unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, -1, d)
        selected = x.gather(1, idx)                 # only k tokens get compute
        processed = self.block(selected) - selected  # block residual delta
        w = scores.gather(1, top).unsqueeze(-1)     # router weight keeps gradient
        out = x.clone()
        out.scatter_(1, idx, selected + w * processed)
        return out                                  # skipped tokens unchanged

y = MoDBlock()(torch.randn(2, 64, 512))

ringattn.d:
Ring Attention computes exact attention over sequences too long for one device by splitting the sequence into blocks across devices arranged in a ring and passing key-value blocks around that ring. Each device keeps its own query block fixed and, in successive steps, receives the next device's key and value block while sending its current one onward.

At each step, a device computes blockwise attention between its queries and the key-value block it currently holds, combining partial results exactly with the online softmax used in FlashAttention. After as many steps as there are devices, every query block has attended to the whole sequence. Communication of the next block is overlapped with computation on the current one. Memory per device scales with the block size, not the full sequence, allowing contexts of millions of tokens. For causal models, naive splitting causes load imbalance because later blocks attend to more tokens, which striped or zigzag orderings are used to fix.
ringattn.f: m ← max(m, rowmax(S_j)); ℓ ← e^{m_old−m}ℓ + rowsum(e^{S_j−m}); O ← e^{m_old−m}O + e^{S_j−m}V_j

The approach keeps attention exact while memory per GPU stays bounded. They use a zigzag token ordering so that causal masking does not leave some GPUs idle.

import torch

def ring_attention(q_blocks, k_blocks, v_blocks):
    """Simulate N devices; device i owns q_blocks[i] and passes K/V around."""
    n = len(q_blocks)
    outs = []
    for i in range(n):                                # each device in parallel
        q = q_blocks[i]; m = torch.full((q.shape[0], 1), float("-inf"))
        l, o = torch.zeros(q.shape[0], 1), torch.zeros_like(q)
        for step in range(n):                         # receive next K/V block
            j = (i + step) % n
            s = q @ k_blocks[j].T / q.shape[-1] ** 0.5
            m_new = torch.maximum(m, s.max(dim=-1, keepdim=True).values)
            p = torch.exp(s - m_new)
            scale = torch.exp(m - m_new)              # rescale old accumulators
            l = scale * l + p.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
            o, m = scale * o + p @ v_blocks[j], m_new
        outs.append(o / l)
    return torch.cat(outs)

q, k, v = (torch.randn(4 * 32, 64) for _ in range(3))
out = ring_attention(q.chunk(4), k.chunk(4), v.chunk(4))
ref = torch.softmax(q @ k.T / 8, dim=-1) @ v
assert torch.allclose(out, ref, atol=1e-4)            # exact attention

multimodal.d:
A multimodal LLM is a language model that can take inputs in more than one modality, such as images, audio or video, alongside text, and reason over them jointly. The most common design connects a pretrained vision encoder to a pretrained LLM through a projector that maps image patch features into the LLM's token embedding space.

The image becomes a sequence of visual tokens placed in the prompt next to text tokens, so the LLM attends over both with its usual machinery. Training typically has two stages: aligning the projector on image-caption pairs, then instruction tuning on visual question answering, document and chart data. Some models instead train natively multimodal from the start, or use cross-attention layers to inject visual features. Common weaknesses include hallucinating objects that are not present, difficulty with fine detail when images are downscaled, and weak counting or spatial reasoning, so high-resolution tiling and careful evaluation matter.

Answering questions about charts and screenshots
Visual assistance and image description

A vision-language-action model is a robot policy built on a pretrained vision-language model that takes camera images and a natural-language instruction as input and outputs robot actions. Examples include RT-2, OpenVLA and Physical Intelligence's π0.

The key idea is to reuse the visual and semantic knowledge of a large web-trained model for control. Actions, such as end-effector position changes and gripper state, are either discretized into bins and emitted as special tokens, like words, or produced by a continuous action head such as a diffusion or flow-matching decoder, which handles smooth, high-frequency motion better. Models are fine-tuned on large datasets of robot demonstrations collected across many robots and tasks. This gives better generalization to new objects and instructions than policies trained from scratch. Major limitations are inference latency relative to control rates, which is why action chunks are often predicted at once, the high cost of collecting demonstration data, and the safety risks of deploying learned policies on physical hardware.

worldmodel.d:
A world model is a learned model of an environment's dynamics that predicts how the state of the world will change in response to actions, allowing an agent to simulate outcomes before acting. Typically an encoder compresses observations into a latent state, a dynamics model predicts the next latent state given an action, and decoders predict rewards or reconstruct observations.

Agents can then plan or learn policies inside this imagined environment. The Dreamer family trains actor and critic networks entirely on imagined latent rollouts, which is far more sample-efficient than learning from real interaction alone, and MuZero plans with a learned model through tree search. Large video-generation models are also studied as world models. The central limitation is compounding error: small prediction mistakes accumulate over long imagined horizons, and agents can exploit model inaccuracies, learning behaviors that work only in the imperfect simulation.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class LatentWorldModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, obs_dim=64, act_dim=4, z=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(obs_dim, 128), nn.ELU(), nn.Linear(128, z))
        self.dyn = nn.GRUCell(z + act_dim, z)            # latent transition
        self.reward, self.dec = nn.Linear(z, 1), nn.Linear(z, obs_dim)  # reward + recon heads

    def imagine(self, z, policy, horizon=15):
        rewards = []
        for _ in range(horizon):                         # rollout without the real env
            a = policy(z)
            z = self.dyn(torch.cat([z, a], -1), z)
            rewards.append(self.reward(z))
        return torch.stack(rewards).sum(0)

wm = LatentWorldModel()
policy = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(32, 4), nn.Tanh())
obs, act, next_obs = torch.randn(16, 64), torch.randn(16, 4), torch.randn(16, 64)
z = wm.enc(obs)
z_next = wm.dyn(torch.cat([z, act], -1), z)
model_loss = ((wm.dec(z_next) - next_obs) ** 2).mean()   # learn dynamics
imagined_return = wm.imagine(z.detach(), policy).mean()  # train policy in imagination

jepa.d:
A Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture is a self-supervised learning approach, proposed at Meta, that predicts the representation of a missing part of the input from the representation of a visible part, rather than reconstructing raw pixels or tokens. I-JEPA applies it to images and V-JEPA to video.

A context encoder processes the visible regions, a target encoder, which is an exponential moving average of the context encoder, embeds the masked target regions, and a predictor maps context embeddings plus target positions to predicted target embeddings. The loss is the distance between predicted and actual target embeddings. Because the model predicts in abstract representation space, it can ignore unpredictable low-level detail, such as exact texture, and focus on semantic structure, which yields strong features for downstream tasks with efficient training. The main risk is representation collapse, where all inputs map to the same embedding and the loss becomes trivially zero; the EMA target encoder and stop-gradient are used to prevent it.

Feature extraction for low-label downstream tasks

import torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

d, n_patches = 256, 64

target_enc = copy.deepcopy(context_enc).requires_grad_(False)   # EMA copy
predictor = nn.TransformerEncoder(nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d, 8, batch_first=True), 2)

kan.d:
A Kolmogorov–Arnold Network is a neural network in which the learnable nonlinear functions sit on the edges between neurons rather than as fixed activations on the nodes. Each edge applies its own learned univariate function, and each node simply sums its incoming edge outputs.

The design is inspired by the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem, which states that any continuous multivariate function can be written as sums and compositions of univariate functions. An MLP instead learns linear edge weights with fixed node activations. Because each learned edge function is a one-dimensional curve, KANs can be visualized, pruned and sometimes matched to symbolic formulas, which makes them attractive for scientific discovery on small, smooth problems such as fitting physical laws. Their main limitations are practical: spline evaluation is slower and less GPU-friendly than matrix multiplication, and on large-scale tasks like language or vision, KANs have not shown clear advantages over MLPs at equal parameter or compute budgets.

Interpretable fitting of smooth scientific data
Small-scale function approximation and PDE solving

They then replace those edges with symbolic expressions to recover a compact formula. For their larger prediction models they still use standard MLPs because of speed.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class KANLayer(nn.Module):
    """Each edge i->j has its own learnable 1D function (RBF basis here)."""
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_out, n_basis=8, x_range=(-2, 2)):
        super().__init__()
        self.register_buffer("centers", torch.linspace(*x_range, n_basis))
        self.width = (x_range[1] - x_range[0]) / (n_basis - 1)
        self.coef = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(d_in, d_out, n_basis) * 0.1)  # phi_ij
        self.base = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(d_in, d_out) * 0.1)          # SiLU residual

    def forward(self, x):                                     # x: (B, d_in)
        basis = torch.exp(-((x[..., None] - self.centers) / self.width) ** 2)
        spline = torch.einsum("bik,iok->bo", basis, self.coef)  # sum over edges
        return spline + F.silu(x) @ self.base

model = nn.Sequential(KANLayer(2, 5), KANLayer(5, 1))
x = torch.rand(256, 2) * 4 - 2
y = torch.sin(torch.pi * x[:, :1]) + x[:, 1:] ** 2           # target function
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
for _ in range(500):
    loss = F.mse_loss(model(x), y)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

ttt.d:
Test-time training updates some of a model's parameters on each test input, using a self-supervised objective, before or while making a prediction. Since no labels are available at test time, the model minimizes an auxiliary loss, and the adapted weights are then used for the actual task.

The idea originated as a way to handle distribution shift: if a test image is corrupted differently from training data, a few gradient steps on a rotation-prediction or masked-reconstruction task adapt the shared features to it. Later, in TTT layers, the hidden state of a sequence layer is itself a small model whose weights are updated by gradient steps on each token. In reasoning tasks such as ARC, models are fine-tuned on the examples given in each problem before answering. The costs are extra computation and latency per input, and if the auxiliary task is poorly aligned with the main task, adaptation can make predictions worse.

import copy
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

encoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 32))
decoder = nn.Linear(32, 64)        # self-supervised head (reconstruction)
classifier = nn.Linear(32, 10)     # main task head

def predict_with_ttt(x, steps=5, lr=1e-3):
    enc = copy.deepcopy(encoder)   # adapt a copy for this test input only
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(enc.parameters(), lr=lr)
    for _ in range(steps):
        x_noisy = x + 0.1 * torch.randn_like(x)
        loss = F.mse_loss(decoder(enc(x_noisy)), x)   # no labels needed
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return classifier(enc(x)).argmax(-1)          # predict with adapted weights

x_test = torch.randn(1, 64)        # a shifted test example
pred = predict_with_ttt(x_test)

merging.d:
Model merging combines the weights of several models fine-tuned from the same base model into a single model, without additional training, so that it inherits the abilities of each. The simplest form averages weights; more effective methods operate on task vectors, the difference between a fine-tuned model's weights and the base weights.

Task arithmetic adds scaled task vectors to the base model. TIES-Merging reduces interference by trimming small changes, resolving sign conflicts between task vectors by majority sign, and averaging only agreeing values. DARE randomly drops a large share of delta parameters and rescales the rest before merging. Merging is cheap, needs no training data, and is popular for combining skills in open models. The key requirement is a shared base model: models trained from different initializations generally lie in different regions of weight space, and averaging them produces a broken model. Even with a shared base, merged skills often trade off, so evaluation on each task is essential.
u: Combining coding and math fine-tunes
Merging LoRA adapters for multiple domains
Averaging checkpoints for robustness (model soups)
merging.x: An open-source team merges a math fine-tune and a coding fine-tune of the same base model with TIES-Merging, using mergekit. The merged model is evaluated on both benchmark suites plus general chat quality before release. Several merge weightings are tried, since the best values differ across task combinations.

import torch

def ties_merge(base, finetuned, density=0.2, lam=1.0):
    """TIES merge of state_dicts that share the same base model."""
    merged = {}
    for name, w0 in base.items():
        deltas = torch.stack([ft[name] - w0 for ft in finetuned])   # task vectors
        # 1) trim: keep only the top-density fraction by magnitude
        k = max(1, int(density * deltas[0].numel()))
        thresh = deltas.abs().flatten(1).kthvalue(deltas[0].numel() - k + 1, dim=1).values
        deltas = deltas * (deltas.abs() >= thresh.view(-1, *[1] * w0.dim()))
        # 2) elect sign by summed magnitude, 3) average only agreeing values
        sign = torch.sign(deltas.sum(0))
        agree = (torch.sign(deltas) == sign) & (deltas != 0)
        merged_delta = (deltas * agree).sum(0) / agree.sum(0).clamp(min=1)
        merged[name] = w0 + lam * merged_delta
    return merged

base = {"w": torch.randn(16, 16)}
fts = [{"w": base["w"] + 0.01 * torch.randn(16, 16)} for _ in range(3)]
merged = ties_merge(base, fts)

bitnet.d:
BitNet is a family of language model architectures that train transformers with extremely low-precision weights from scratch, rather than quantizing a full-precision model afterward. BitNet b1.58 constrains every weight in its linear layers to one of three values, −1, 0 or +1, which carries about 1.58 bits of information per weight.

During training, full-precision latent weights are kept for the optimizer, and in the forward pass they are scaled by their mean absolute value, rounded and clipped to the ternary set; gradients pass through the rounding with a straight-through estimator. Activations are quantized to 8 bits. With ternary weights, matrix multiplication reduces mainly to additions and subtractions, which greatly lowers memory, bandwidth and energy. Reported results show BitNet b1.58 approaching full-precision quality at billions of parameters. The main limitations are that models must be trained this way from the start, and current GPUs lack native ternary arithmetic, so speedups depend on specialized kernels or future hardware.

On-device inference with tight memory budgets
Energy-efficient large-scale model serving
